periods.activity_title: Meet the Frog: Read-Aloud and First Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.56): answer questions on where the frog sits and how it catches food.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively while students follow in their textbooks (pp.55–56). After the first read, students echo-read two stanzas together, paying attention to the bouncy rhythm of the couplets.
Shared re-reading of the poem — teacher and students read aloud together. Students note any word or image that surprises them and share one observation with a neighbour.

Let us Think — A. ("questions on the frog's home and food-catching"). Teacher poses the first two questions from the exercise and students discuss answers in pairs before sharing with the class; teacher records key words on the board.
Quick whole-class consolidation: teacher asks students to name one place the frog lives and one way it catches food, drawing on words from the poem they have just read.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's darting-tongue and webbed-feet images give students concrete anchors for the comprehension questions — invite students to locate those lines before answering. The remaining two questions from the exercise (on movement and camouflage) are well-suited for the next sitting on this spine; flag them briefly for students who wish to explore ahead.

periods.activity_title: Deeper into the Poem: Movement and Camouflage

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.56): answer questions on how the frog moves and what helps it hide.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites a volunteer to read the third and fourth stanzas of the poem aloud (pp.55–56). The class listens for the two images the stanzas contain — camouflage and the threat from snakes — and names them aloud.

Let us Think — A. ("questions on the frog's movement and camouflage"). Teacher poses the remaining two comprehension questions; students discuss in pairs and then share full-sentence answers with the class. Teacher writes key vocabulary (webbed feet, camouflage, dew) on the board.

Whole-class discussion: teacher asks students to explain in their own words why the frog's colour helps it survive, connecting the poem's image of matching plants and leaves to real-world camouflage. Students may illustrate their reasoning with a quick sketch.
Closing reflection: each student says one thing they found surprising about the frog's life based on what was read and discussed today, in a round-the-room share.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the poem together and discussed the frog's tongue and habitat, students are now ready to push into the poem's more nuanced ideas — colour-matching as survival and the contrast between pride and danger. Encourage students to point to specific lines rather than paraphrase loosely.

periods.activity_title: Talk Like a Frog: Discussion and Tongue Twisters

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak (p.56): discuss living like a frog and comparing frogs with fish.
Let us Speak — A. (p.58): practise tongue twisters with frog-themed alliteration, increasing speed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the poem's central image — the frog hopping between pond and land — and asks students to close their eyes and imagine being that frog for thirty seconds. One or two students share their mental picture.

Let us Think + Let us Speak ("discuss living like a frog and comparing frogs with fish"). Teacher poses the four discussion prompts in pairs, then invites one pair per question to share with the class; teacher scaffolds with guiding questions about land-and-water life.

Let us Speak — A. ("tongue twisters with frog-themed alliteration"). Teacher models the first tongue twister slowly, then the class repeats as a group, gradually speeding up. Each twister is practised three rounds — slow, medium, fast — and students count how many clean repetitions they can achieve.
Cool-down: students vote on which tongue twister was hardest and explain why — teacher notes the sounds that caused trouble, drawing attention to the repeated 'fr' cluster.

periods.teacher_notes: The discussion prompts build on the poem's imagery of webbed feet and dual habitat — students can draw on those lines directly rather than speaking in the abstract. The tongue twisters' repeated 'fr' cluster will naturally lead into word-work on consonant patterns.

periods.activity_title: Listen, Draw and Share: My Frog's World

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (p.60): follow teacher's instructions to draw and label a frog's world setting.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the opening two stanzas of the poem slowly, once, so students hold the poem's landscape — pond, muddy drain, dew, grass — in mind before the listening activity begins.

Teacher reads the 'My Frog's World' instructions aloud, step by step (p.60), pausing after each instruction for students to act on it. Students draw the place where their frog lives, following the oral directions.

Teacher reads the instructions again, then students draw their frog inside the setting and write at least two words from the poem around the drawing as labels. Teacher circulates and reads the oral prompts a third time for those who need it.

Students colour their drawings and write one short sentence of their own about their frog's world in the space provided. Teacher invites three or four volunteers to hold up their work and describe what their frog is doing in one sentence.
Whole-class share: teacher asks students which poem words they chose as labels and writes a selection on the board, celebrating the variety of images students selected.

periods.teacher_notes: This listening activity is designed for oral instruction — the teacher reads each step, repeating it three to four times as NCF guidance recommends, so students respond to voice rather than print. Students' labelling choices reveal which poem images made the strongest impression.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.57): fill in conjunctions (and, but, because, or) in frog-themed sentences.
Let us Learn — B. (pp.57–58): rearrange jumbled words into correct sentences about animals.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the line 'I live on land and water too' from the poem on the board and asks students what the word 'and' does in that sentence. Through brief class discussion, teacher introduces the idea that joining words connect ideas — then adds 'but', 'because', and 'or' to the board with quick examples.

Let us Learn — A. ("fill in conjunctions in frog-themed sentences"). Teacher reads each sentence aloud, students choose the correct joining word from the brackets and write it in. After each answer, the class reads the completed sentence aloud to check it sounds right.

Let us Learn — B. ("rearrange jumbled words into correct sentences about animals"). Teacher reads the jumbled words for the first item aloud and asks students what the sentence is likely to be about before they arrange it. Students work independently on all five items, then pairs compare answers.

Whole-class check: teacher reads one correct sentence for each item and students identify the joining word or the position of the adverb that makes the sentence work. Any common errors from pair comparison are addressed here.

periods.teacher_notes: Rooting the conjunction work in the poem's own lines — 'I live on land and water too', 'I croak my songs, they sound so loud' — helps students see grammar as a live tool rather than an abstract rule. The sentence-rearrangement task extends the idea of word order, which students can test by reading their versions aloud.

periods.activity_title: Write Back to Hopper the Frog

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.55–64): plan, draft and share a reply letter to Hopper the frog.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Hopper's letter aloud from the textbook, pausing to highlight the letter's features: greeting, self-introduction, personal detail, question to the reader, and sign-off. Class identifies these parts together.

Modelled writing: teacher thinks aloud while writing the first two sentences of a reply on the board — greeting Hopper, then sharing one thing the teacher herself likes to do. Students suggest ideas for the second sentence, seeing how a writer makes choices.

Students plan their own reply using the five features identified earlier: greeting, a sentence about themselves, something they enjoy, an answer to Hopper's question, and a sign-off. They draft the full letter in their notebooks, aiming for four to six sentences.
Pair share: students read their letters aloud to a partner. The partner checks that all five parts of a letter are present and gives one word of positive feedback.

Two or three volunteers read their letters to the class. Teacher highlights one strong personal detail from each letter that would make Hopper curious — connecting writing back to oracy and the idea of audience.

periods.teacher_notes: Hopper's letter gives students a concrete model to respond to, so modelling can focus on choices rather than mechanics. Encourage students to draw on the poem's world — ponds, croaking, rain, insects — when describing what they imagine Hopper's life is like.

periods.activity_title: Hidden Frogs, Draw a Duck and a Fishy Puzzle

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do — A. (p.62): find five hidden frogs in the nature-scene picture.
Let us Do — B. (p.63): follow the five-step diagram to draw a duck in the given space.

homework.task_brief: Let us Explore (pp.55–64): choose any two water creatures from the list and find two or three facts about each to share next time.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do — A. ("find five hidden frogs in the nature-scene picture"). Students open to page 62 and search independently for the hidden frogs, circling each one they find. Teacher then leads a class reveal, asking students to describe exactly where each frog is hidden — above, below, behind — building observational language.

Let us Do — B. ("follow the five-step diagram to draw a duck"). Teacher walks through each of the five steps in the diagram on page 63 on the board before students attempt their own. Students draw their duck step by step in the given space, at a comfortable pace.

Let us Do — C. (p.64): teacher presents the crayon-fish puzzle to the class and invites students to try moving exactly three crayons to change the direction the fish is swimming. Students work in small groups, physically arranging pencils or crayons on their desks to solve it.

Groups share their solutions and explain their reasoning. Teacher closes by connecting the puzzle's logical thinking to the way the frog poem surprised readers — both the fish puzzle and the poem show that things are not always what they first appear.

periods.teacher_notes: The hidden-frog search connects naturally to the poem's camouflage stanza — students who recall 'I hide so well in grass and leaves' will find the activity richly grounded. The duck-drawing task develops careful sequential observation, a skill that complements the close reading students have practised throughout the poem.
materials: Crayons or coloured pencils (for the fish-direction puzzle)

items.source_context: Frog's habitat (ponds, drains, dew), tongue-flicking to catch food, webbed feet, camouflage in leaves.
items.item_stem: The poem tells us that the frog hides by matching its surroundings. Which two things does the frog's colour match?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this may be thinking of muddy environments described elsewhere in the poem rather than the camouflage stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a student who has associated the frog's habitats with its hiding strategy, confusing where it lives with what it hides among.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student has connected 'Up I go into the sky' with camouflage rather than reading the specific camouflage lines.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves explicit information and explains key details using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Frog's habitat (ponds, drains, dew), tongue-flicking to catch food, webbed feet, camouflage in leaves.
items.item_stem: The frog in the poem lives in two different environments and has special body parts that help it survive. In two or three sentences, explain where the frog lives and describe two features of its body that help it in those places.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The frog lives both on land and in water, in places like ponds, muddy drains, and grassy areas with dew. Its webbed feet help it swim easily in water, and its tongue flicks out very fast to catch insects for food.

items.source_lo: Student expresses personal response and comparisons through guided spoken discussion using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Frog's amphibious life, comparison with fish, webbed feet versus scuba flippers, imaginative play.
items.item_stem: The poem says the frog lives on land and in water. A fish lives only in water. Which statement below correctly states a difference between a frog's life and a fish's life?

options.text: A fish has webbed feet to help it move, just like a frog.
A frog can hop on land, but a fish cannot leave the water.
Both the frog and the fish croak to communicate.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true — the poem shows the frog hopping on land and swimming in water, while a fish cannot leave water. Statement 2 is false — it is the frog, not the fish, that has webbed feet. Statement 3 is false — only the frog croaks; croaking is not mentioned as a fish behaviour.

items.source_lo: Student expresses personal response and comparisons through guided spoken discussion using a poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Frog's amphibious life, comparison with fish, webbed feet versus scuba flippers, imaginative play.
items.item_stem: The poem describes the frog as proud, joyful, and full of energy as it leaps and croaks. Imagine you could spend one day living like the frog in the poem. Speak for about a minute: where would you go, what would you do, and how would you feel?

expected_elements: Names a specific place from the poem's world.
Describes at least one frog-like action clearly.
Expresses a personal feeling with a reason.

items.source_context: Reply to Hopper the frog's letter — personal hobbies, eating habits, and life in a pond.
items.item_stem: Hopper the frog says his favourite hobby is sitting in water puddles and croaking. Write ONE sentence telling Hopper what your favourite hobby is, as if you were writing in a letter to him.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any clearly written sentence that names a specific hobby and is addressed to Hopper in a friendly tone, for example: 'My favourite hobby is painting pictures of animals, and I would love to paint you one day!'

items.item_stem: Write a short reply letter to Hopper the frog. Include a greeting, share one thing you enjoy doing, ask Hopper one question about his life in the pond, and end with a proper sign-off. Write four to six sentences.

expected_elements: Greeting names Hopper and sounds friendly.
Shares a personal detail or hobby clearly.
Asks Hopper a genuine question about pond life.

items.item_stem: Choose the correct conjunction to complete each sentence about the frog.
items.visual_stimulus:
| # | Sentence | Conjunction choices |
|---|----------|--------------------|
| 1 | The frog is small _______ very fast. | (and / because) |
| 2 | The frog hides well _______ its colours match the leaves. | (or / because) |
| 3 | Would you like to see a frog _______ a tadpole? | (but / or) |
| 4 | The frog croaks loudly _______ snakes can hear it. | (but / so) |

items.item_stem: Use the conjunction 'because' to write one sentence of your own that explains something the frog from the poem can do well. Say your sentence aloud clearly.

expected_elements: Uses 'because' correctly to join two ideas.
Names a frog ability from the poem.
Sentence is spoken clearly and completely.

items.item_stem: Match each description on the left with the activity it belongs to on the right.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Description | Activity |
|-------------|----------|
| 1. You look very carefully for creatures hiding among leaves and grass. | A. Drawing a duck step by step |
| 2. You follow numbered picture instructions to make a shape grow. | B. Finding hidden frogs in a nature scene |
| 3. You move only three objects to change the way something points. | C. The fish-direction crayon puzzle |

answer_key.left: 1. You look very carefully for creatures hiding among leaves and grass.
answer_key.right: B. Finding hidden frogs in a nature scene

answer_key.left: 2. You follow numbered picture instructions to make a shape grow.
answer_key.right: A. Drawing a duck step by step

answer_key.left: 3. You move only three objects to change the way something points.

items.item_stem: The poem says the frog hides so well that it is very hard to spot it. Think about the hidden-frog picture activity. Speak for about a minute: what did you look for to find the hidden frogs, and what made the search tricky?

expected_elements: Describes a specific visual clue they searched for.
Explains why camouflage made finding frogs hard.
Connects observation to the poem's hiding stanza.
